subject: Agriculture
title: Soy and Deforestation
description: A fast breakdown of Soy and Deforestation for builders.

hook.text: The Amazon isn't being cleared for burgers directly. It's being cleared for soy—to feed livestock.

buildup.text: Soy is the world's main protein feed for chickens, pigs, and farmed fish. Demand has exploded.

discovery.text: Brazil became the world's largest soy exporter, converting forest and cerrado savanna into soy fields.

twist.text: About 77% of global soy goes to animal feed. Only 7% is eaten directly by humans as tofu or soy milk.

climax.text: Reducing meat demand would cut soy demand—and forest destruction—more than any conservation law could.

punchline.text: The forest falls for feed, not food.

quiz.question: What percentage of global soy is used for animal feed?

details.summary: Soybean cultivation is a leading driver of tropical deforestation, especially in South America, where it expands to feed livestock worldwide. This topic examines the soy-livestock-deforestation connection, the Amazon Soy Moratorium, and paths to deforestation-free supply chains.
details.whyItMatters: About 75% of global soy becomes animal feed. The demand for cheap livestock feed drives forest clearing in the Amazon and Cerrado, accelerating biodiversity loss and climate change.
takeaways: Brazil is the world's largest soybean exporter, with much production on former forest land
About 75% of global soy production is used for livestock feed, not human food
The Amazon Soy Moratorium since 2006 reduced deforestation for soy in the Amazon biome

faq.question: How does soy production drive deforestation?
faq.answer: Growing global demand for cheap livestock feed—primarily soy—incentivizes clearing tropical forests and savanna in Brazil, Argentina, and Paraguay. Forests are converted to farmland either directly for soy or indirectly as soy farms push ranchers deeper into forests.

faq.question: What is the Amazon Soy Moratorium?
faq.answer: Agreed in 2006, major traders committed not to purchase soy grown on newly deforested Amazon land. It successfully reduced deforestation for soy in the Amazon biome, but critics note it shifted clearing to the Cerrado savanna, which lacks similar protections.
